readings.title: A bakery changes its queue
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A small bakery noticed a long morning queue. The owner considered hiring another cashier, although customers said the wait felt confusing. The main obstacle was one line serving two different kinds of order. People collecting prepaid bread waited behind customers choosing several items for the first time. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a week of queue observations. Staff recorded arrival times and asked customers whether they were collecting or making a new purchase. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated prepaid collections took very little time. The bottleneck came from mixing quick collections with longer orders, not from the total number of customers. The group then introduced a marked collection point. The bakery set aside a small counter space for prepaid orders and kept the main line for new purchases. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: a process can improve before staffing grows. Understanding the kinds of tasks in a queue helped the owner respond without assuming that more workers were the only answer. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a bakery changes its queue, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Plain return rules for a repair shop
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An electronics repair shop gave customers a long printed notice. People still called to ask when they could collect an item. The main obstacle was return rules hidden in dense wording. The notice mixed payment, collection and warranty details in one paragraph with several unfamiliar terms. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used customer questions sorted by purpose. Workers kept a list of repeated calls and asked a few new customers to locate the collection date on the notice. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated collection information was hardest to find. Customers understood the repair itself but missed the sentence explaining how they would receive an update. The group then introduced short headings and a dated message. The shop separated the rules into clear sections and sent each customer a direct collection update. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: consumer information should answer real questions. A complete notice is not effective if the detail people need remains difficult to find. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in plain return rules for a repair shop, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Sharing a market delivery space
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Several small market sellers received goods at the same entrance. Deliveries often blocked shoppers because arrival times were unplanned. The main obstacle was overlapping delivery vans at a narrow gate. Individual sellers each chose a convenient hour, but the shared space could not safely hold several vehicles at once. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a common arrival calendar. Sellers listed delivery needs, and the market manager offered short time slots during less busy periods. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated most sellers could shift by half an hour. Only one fresh-food stall needed a special early slot, which the group could accommodate without losing fairness. The group then introduced scheduled unloading with one stated exception. The manager marked a loading point and explained the rule to drivers before the next market day. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: shared resources need visible coordination. A simple schedule protected both trading activity and the movement of customers. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in sharing a market delivery space, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A price label that includes the total
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A craft stall displayed the base price of personalised gifts. Buyers were surprised when a small finishing charge appeared at payment. The main obstacle was unclear final prices for customised items. The seller had listed each extra fee separately, but customers could not easily calculate the total while choosing. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a trial of examples beside products. The stall showed common combinations with full prices and asked visitors to estimate the cost before ordering. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated complete examples reduced misunderstandings. Customers still valued choice, but they wanted to see typical total costs without asking repeated questions. The group then introduced clear examples and a written final quote. Staff displayed sample totals and confirmed the exact price before making a personalised item. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: transparent prices support confident choices. A seller can offer options while making the likely cost understandable from the start. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a price label that includes the total, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the local business support programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about small businesses and consumers, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关小微经营与消费者体验的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the business support desk suggesting a practical change to the local business support programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the local business support programme. People have noticed one line serving two different kinds of order, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
